paper.title: The long-term impact of Danish vulnerable neighbourhoods in adolescence on employment status in emerging adulthood
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 13), verbatim: "The data used in the present paper cannot be shared publicly due to legal and ethical restrictions pertaining to Danish register-based data but can be obtained by application to Statistics …

registers.name_in_paper: register data of the Danish population (Statistics Denmark), with information on demographic and socioeconomic characteristics
variables_mentioned: number of children in the family

registers.name_in_paper: Socioeconomic Classification (SOCIO13) variable by Statistics Denmark
unique family ID from Statistics Denmark (families defined as a single person or couple with or without children living at the same address)

georeferenced micro-areas (Lund, 2018): data dividing the Danish population into micro-areas created with an automated redistricting algorithm, smallest areas with at least 100 residents and 50 households separated by large physical barriers
Danish governmental list of particularly vulnerable housing areas, October 2010 (the 2010 'ghetto' list; Regeringen, 2010), 29 areas
Statistics Denmark definitions of immigrants, descendants and persons of Danish origin (Statistics Denmark, 2017)

linkages: Individuals linked to their families through a unique family ID from Statistics Denmark, with families defined as a single person or couple with or without children living at the same address
Individuals and families nested in previously developed georeferenced micro-area neighbourhoods (Lund, 2018) via the registered address

Vulnerable-neighbourhood exposure assigned by matching the individuals' registered addresses in December 2009 to the 29 areas on the October 2010 governmental list; the exact property boundaries differ slightly from the micro-area delineations, with an average of 1.59 micro-areas per vulnerable neighbourhood
Individuals followed from 2009 to 2019 in the registers to observe employment status at age 20-25

sample.universe: The Danish adolescent population aged 10-15 in December 2009, born between 1994 and 1999, including immigrants who were not born in Denmark
sample.unit_of_observation: individual (level 1), nested in families (level 2), nested in neighbourhoods / micro-areas (level 3)
selection_rules: All Danish adolescents aged 10-15 years living at home in 2009 (N = 410,952)
Exclude individuals not residing in Denmark at age 20-25 years in 2019 (N = 9,047), leaving individuals living in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019 (N = 401,905)

Exclude individuals with missing information on occupational status (N = 43), micro-areas (N = 10,515), vulnerable neighbourhoods (N = 57) and family variables (N = 716); missing data were omitted and not imputed
Study sample with complete data (N = 390,574), nested in 301,227 families and 7,937 neighbourhoods
Individuals not living at home with one or both parents were excluded, because selection into vulnerable neighbourhoods could not be controlled for on the young person's family characteristics
All models are stratified by native Danes (N = 352,820) and immigrants/descendants (N = 37,041)
sample.n_individuals: 390,574 individuals in 301,227 families in 7,937 neighbourhoods (352,820 of Danish origin; 37,041 immigrants and descendants)

construction_notes: Outcome: SOCIO13 (most important source of income or employment in 2019) dichotomised into 1 = not in education or employment and 0 = employed, self-employed or in education; exact codes in Supporting Information Table S1

Exposure: binary indicator for residence in December 2009 in one of the 29 areas of the October 2010 governmental list of particularly vulnerable housing areas; 0.40% of native Danes and 15.97% of immigrants and descendants were exposed
Family income: total sum of the annual disposable income in the family, entered in quartiles in Tables 1-2
Family education: highest level of education attained in the family, ISCED categorised into basic (levels 0-2), medium (levels 3-5) and high (levels 6-8)
Family unemployment: three categories (no parent(s), one parent, both parents unemployed); unemployment includes recipients of sickness benefits, persons on leave and recipients of cash benefits
Family type: married, cohabiting or single-parent family. Children in the family: only child, 2, 3-4, more than 4

Country of origin collapsed into Western (the 28 EU countries plus Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, Vatican State, Canada, USA, Australia and New Zealand) and non-Western (all other countries), following the Statistics Denmark procedure

Micro-areas: smallest possible areas with at least 100 residents and 50 households, separated by large physical barriers, built with an automated redistricting algorithm (Lund, 2018); mean 1.3 observations per family and 49.2 per neighbourhood
Age entered as fixed effects, i.e. dummy variables representing the birth cohorts
ICC computed by the latent-variable method with level-1 variance pi squared / 3 (approximately 3.29); MOR = exp(sqrt(2 x Var) x Phi^-1(0.75)); PCV = (Var_empty - Var_model)/Var_empty

The SOCIO13 and FAMILIE_ID dst_code mappings (IND, BEF) follow the Statistics Denmark documentation URLs the article cites (personindkomst/socio13 and moduldata-for-befolkning-og-valg/familie-id); the article itself names no register codes

claims.statement: Among persons of Danish origin, living in a vulnerable neighbourhood in adolescence (2009) rather than a non-vulnerable neighbourhood is associated with a higher probability of not being in education or employment at age 20-25 in 2019 (OR, Model 1).

treatment.label: Living in a vulnerable neighbourhood in adolescence (2010 Danish governmental ‘ghetto’ list area)

register_source.value: Danish governmental list of particularly vulnerable housing areas, October 2010 (Regeringen, 2010), linked to Statistics Denmark registered addresses in December 2009

definition.value: Binary indicator equal to 1 if the adolescent's registered address in December 2009 fell in one of the 29 areas on the Danish governmental list of particularly vulnerable housing areas of October 2010 (the 2010 ‘ghetto’ list), and 0 otherwise; non-vulnerable neighbourhood is the reference category.

timing.value: Measured in December 2009, at ages 10–15 (adolescence)

outcome.label: Not being in education or employment in emerging adulthood (NEET), age 20–25

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark Socioeconomic Classification (SOCIO13), 2019

definition.value: Binary indicator built from the SOCIO13 socioeconomic classification, which records the most important source of income or employment for the person in 2019. Coded 1 for individuals not in education or employment and 0 for individuals who were employed, self-employed or in education (exact codes in Supporting Information Table S1).

timing.value: Measured in 2019, at age 20–25, ten years after the exposure measurement in December 2009

units.value: odds ratio relative to the reference category 'Non-vulnerable neighbourhood'

estimand.target_population: Persons of Danish origin (native Danes: at least one parent a Danish citizen and born in Denmark) among Danish adolescents aged 10–15 and living at home with one or both parents in December 2009 (born 1994–1999) who were resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019
estimand.time_horizon: Ten years: exposure measured in December 2009 at age 10–15, outcome measured in 2019 at age 20–25

population.description: Persons of Danish origin (native Danes: at least one parent a Danish citizen and born in Denmark) among Danish adolescents aged 10–15 living at home with one or both parents in December 2009
population.selection: Danish adolescent population aged 10–15 in December 2009 living at home with one or both parents; individuals not residing in Denmark at age 20–25 in 2019 and individuals with missing information on occupational status, micro-area, vulnerable neighbourhood or family variables were excluded (Figure 1).

identification.source_of_variation: Observed cross-sectional variation in December 2009 addresses across the 29 areas on the 2010 Danish governmental list of particularly vulnerable housing areas versus all other micro-areas; no reform, lottery or discontinuity is exploited.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: after conditioning on the individual- and family-level covariates included in the model, the exposure is independent of the potential outcomes for not being in education or employment in 2019.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state that they controlled for a wide range of family characteristics possibly affecting both the selection into vulnerable neighbourhoods and later employment status (p. 12); no balance test or falsification test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No simultaneity / no reverse causation: employment status measured in 2019 cannot have caused the neighbourhood of residence recorded in December 2009.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The ten-year longitudinal design, in which exposure precedes the outcome.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the analysis conditions on adolescents who lived at home with one or both parents in December 2009, were resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, and had complete information on all included register variables.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 (flowchart, p. 4) and the statement that missing data were omitted and not imputed because there were no major differences in age, gender or ethnicity between the study population and the final sample.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unmeasured or residual confounding may remain, so the estimate is not asserted to be a causal effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the discussion as a limitation; no sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The three-level nesting is correctly specified and the family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts are normally distributed and independent of the model covariates.
No interference: one adolescent's neighbourhood exposure does not affect another adolescent's later employment status.
A single baseline measurement adequately captures exposure in adolescence: timing, duration and change of exposure within the two observed time points are not modelled.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Acknowledged as a limitation; a sensitivity analysis restricted to individuals at the same address from 2004 to 2009 is reported as showing no major differences.

threats_discussed: Residual or unmeasured confounding in an observational design, which the authors say limits causal inference
Family-induced selection into vulnerable neighbourhoods (selection bias)
Territorial stigmatisation of the officially designated 'ghetto' areas, which may exacerbate negative influences
Government policies and legislation targeted at the listed areas, which the authors say may lead to an underestimation of the impact of vulnerable neighbourhoods
Only two time periods observed, so timing and cumulative duration of neighbourhood exposure are not captured
Micro-areas may capture the relevant neighbourhood context less well than the areas used in earlier studies
Other relevant contexts (school, region) are not modelled (multi-contextual segregation)
robustness_checks: Sample restricted to individuals who had lived at the same address for five years from 2004 to 2009 (neighbourhood mobility and length of residence)
Outcome redefined as not being in education or employment in two years over 2018-2019 (short- versus long-term employment status)
Tests for interaction effects of gender and of age with vulnerable neighbourhood exposure
Models stratified by the different age groups
Models on the total (non-stratified) sample with an ethnicity x vulnerable neighbourhood interaction (Supporting Information Tables S3-S4, Table S1 and Figure S1)
unresolved_confounders: Potential unmeasured or residual confounding variables (stated by the authors as the reason the causal inferences based on the study are limited)

estimator.value: Three-level random-intercept logistic regression (Stata 17 'melogit'), reported as odds ratios

estimation.specification: logit(Pijk) = log(Pijk/(1 - Pijk)) = b0 + b1*x1ijk + ... + v0k + u0jk, with random intercepts v0k for neighbourhoods (micro-areas) and u0jk for families; Model 1 adjusts for gender, age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the birth cohorts).
fixed_effects: age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the birth cohorts)
controls: age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the birth cohorts)
estimation.clustering: No clustered standard errors are reported; non-independence of individuals in the same family and neighbourhood is handled by the family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts.

source_table.value: Table 2, Danish Origin (N = 352,820) / Model 1 / OR (95% CI), row 'Neighbourhood: Vulnerable neighbourhood'

adjustment_set.label: age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the birth cohorts)
family random intercept (random effect for the family the adolescent lived in in 2009)
neighbourhood random intercept (random effect for the micro-area of residence in 2009)

mediators_claimed: Local work culture, social networks and institutions in the area (named in the introduction as possible mechanisms; not tested)

heterogeneity.dimension: Ethnic origin (models stratified by native Danes versus immigrants and descendants)
heterogeneity.finding: The same OR in Model 1 for immigrants and descendants is 1.63 (1.43, 1.86)***; all models are estimated separately by origin group, and the article reports a significant ethnicity x vulnerable neighbourhood interaction in the non-stratified models indicating a very similar but slightly stronger association for individuals of Danish origin (Supporting Information).

heterogeneity.dimension: Gender and age
heterogeneity.finding: Sensitivity analyses found no interaction effect of gender or age on the association between vulnerable neighbourhoods and employment status.

ambiguities: The title and concluding summary use causal language ('long-term impact', 'can increase the risk'), whereas the results and discussion describe an 'association' and state that the causal inferences based on the study are limited; estimand.type is therefore recorded as descriptive_gap.

evidence.how: Column: Danish Origin (N = 352,820) / Model 1 / OR (95% CI); row: Neighbourhood - Vulnerable neighbourhood
Descriptive Statistics: number (%) and '% Not in education or employment' (measured in 2019) by category of each 2009 covariate, separately for Danish origin and for immigrants and descendants.
Table 2 prints point estimates with 95% confidence intervals and significance stars; no standard errors and no exact p-values are printed anywhere in the article.
No standard deviation of the outcome is printed; Table 1 reports only the percentage not in education or employment by category.
The article never discusses interference between adolescents; the no-interference assumption is implicit in the model.
Statistical significance read from the significance stars printed next to the estimate in Table 2 against the printed note '***p <0.001; **p <0.01; *p <0.05.'

value.as_printed: logit(Pijk ) = log ( Pijk / (1 − Pijk) ) = β0 + β1x1ijk + … + v0k + u0jk
value.lhs: logit(Pijk), the log-odds that individual i in family j in neighbourhood k is not in education or employment in 2019

terms.expression: … (further predictor variables measured for individual i in family j in neighbourhood k)

value.normalisation: Reference (omitted) categories in Table 2: non-vulnerable neighbourhood; boys; basic education (ISCED levels 0–2); family income Q1 (lowest); not unemployed; married; only child; immigrant; Western country of origin. Level-1 variance fixed at π²/3 ≈ 3.29 (standard logistic distribution) for the ICC computation.

theory_referenced: Neighbourhood effects / social ecological model of human development (Bronfenbrenner, 1979)
W. J. Wilson, The Truly Disadvantaged (1987)
Vicious circles of segregation (Tammaru et al., 2021)
General and specific contextual effects (Merlo et al., 2018)

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Overall, the results corroborate the findings of previous multilevel studies (Andersson, 2004; Brattbakk & Wessel, 2013; Urban, 2009).

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Not being in education or employment in two years over the period 2018-2019 (examined in a sensitivity analysis; the paper reports only that there were no major differences and that results are available upon request)

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark population register variables measured in 2009; the article names no register code for this variable

definition.value: Family income in 2009, measured as the total sum of the annual disposable income in the family and entered in quartiles: Q2 versus Q1 (lowest).

timing.value: Measured in 2009, at baseline, when the adolescent was aged 10–15

outcome.label: Not being in education or employment in emerging adulthood (NEET), age 20–25

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark Socioeconomic Classification (SOCIO13), 2019

definition.value: Binary indicator built from the SOCIO13 socioeconomic classification, which records the most important source of income or employment for the person in 2019. Coded 1 for individuals not in education or employment and 0 for individuals who were employed, self-employed or in education (exact codes in Supporting Information Table S1).

timing.value: Measured in 2019, at age 20–25, ten years after the exposure measurement in December 2009

units.value: odds ratio relative to the reference category 'Q1 (lowest)'

estimand.target_population: Persons of Danish origin (native Danes: at least one parent a Danish citizen and born in Denmark) among Danish adolescents aged 10–15 and living at home with one or both parents in December 2009 (born 1994–1999) who were resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019
estimand.time_horizon: Ten years: exposure measured in December 2009 at age 10–15, outcome measured in 2019 at age 20–25

population.description: Persons of Danish origin (native Danes: at least one parent a Danish citizen and born in Denmark) among Danish adolescents aged 10–15 living at home with one or both parents in December 2009
population.selection: Danish adolescent population aged 10–15 in December 2009 living at home with one or both parents; individuals not residing in Denmark at age 20–25 in 2019 and individuals with missing information on occupational status, micro-area, vulnerable neighbourhood or family variables were excluded (Figure 1).

identification.source_of_variation: Observed cross-sectional variation in December 2009 addresses across the 29 areas on the 2010 Danish governmental list of particularly vulnerable housing areas versus all other micro-areas; no reform, lottery or discontinuity is exploited.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: after conditioning on the individual- and family-level covariates included in the model, the exposure is independent of the potential outcomes for not being in education or employment in 2019.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors state that they controlled for a wide range of family characteristics possibly affecting both the selection into vulnerable neighbourhoods and later employment status (p. 12); no balance test or falsification test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: No simultaneity / no reverse causation: employment status measured in 2019 cannot have caused the neighbourhood of residence recorded in December 2009.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The ten-year longitudinal design, in which exposure precedes the outcome.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the analysis conditions on adolescents who lived at home with one or both parents in December 2009, were resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, and had complete information on all included register variables.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 (flowchart, p. 4) and the statement that missing data were omitted and not imputed because there were no major differences in age, gender or ethnicity between the study population and the final sample.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unmeasured or residual confounding may remain, so the estimate is not asserted to be a causal effect.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conceded in the discussion as a limitation; no sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: The three-level nesting is correctly specified and the family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts are normally distributed and independent of the model covariates.
No interference: one adolescent's neighbourhood exposure does not affect another adolescent's later employment status.
A single baseline measurement adequately captures exposure in adolescence: timing, duration and change of exposure within the two observed time points are not modelled.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Acknowledged as a limitation; a sensitivity analysis restricted to individuals at the same address from 2004 to 2009 is reported as showing no major differences.

threats_discussed: Residual or unmeasured confounding in an observational design, which the authors say limits causal inference
Family-induced selection into vulnerable neighbourhoods (selection bias)
Territorial stigmatisation of the officially designated 'ghetto' areas, which may exacerbate negative influences
Government policies and legislation targeted at the listed areas, which the authors say may lead to an underestimation of the impact of vulnerable neighbourhoods
Only two time periods observed, so timing and cumulative duration of neighbourhood exposure are not captured
Micro-areas may capture the relevant neighbourhood context less well than the areas used in earlier studies
Other relevant contexts (school, region) are not modelled (multi-contextual segregation)
robustness_checks: Sample restricted to individuals who had lived at the same address for five years from 2004 to 2009 (neighbourhood mobility and length of residence)
Outcome redefined as not being in education or employment in two years over 2018-2019 (short- versus long-term employment status)
Tests for interaction effects of gender and of age with vulnerable neighbourhood exposure
Models stratified by the different age groups
Models on the total (non-stratified) sample with an ethnicity x vulnerable neighbourhood interaction (Supporting Information Tables S3-S4, Table S1 and Figure S1)
unresolved_confounders: Potential unmeasured or residual confounding variables (stated by the authors as the reason the causal inferences based on the study are limited)

estimator.value: Three-level random-intercept logistic regression (Stata 17 'melogit'), reported as odds ratios

estimation.specification: logit(Pijk) = log(Pijk/(1 - Pijk)) = b0 + b1*x1ijk + ... + v0k + u0jk, with random intercepts v0k for neighbourhoods (micro-areas) and u0jk for families; Model 2 adjusts for gender, age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the birth cohorts), family educational level (ISCED), family income, family unemployment, family type, children in the family.
fixed_effects: age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the birth cohorts)
controls: age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the birth cohorts)
estimation.clustering: No clustered standard errors are reported; non-independence of individuals in the same family and neighbourhood is handled by the family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts.

population.description: Immigrants and descendants among Danish adolescents aged 10–15 living at home with one or both parents in December 2009
population.selection: Danish adolescent population aged 10–15 in December 2009 living at home with one or both parents, resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, with complete information on all included register variables (Figure 1).

identification.source_of_variation: Observed clustering of individuals within 301,227 families and 7,937 georeferenced micro-area neighbourhoods; the quantity is a variance decomposition of a three-level random-intercept logistic model, not an estimate exploiting exogenous variation.

key_assumptions.assumption: The three-level nesting (individuals in families in neighbourhoods) is correctly specified and the family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts are normally distributed and independent of the model covariates.

The intraclass correlation coefficients are computed with the latent-variable method, fixing the level-1 variance at the variance of the standard logistic distribution (pi squared / 3, approximately 3.29).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Snijders and Bosker (1999), cited in the methods.

formal.as_written: ICC (neighbourhood) = Var_neighbourhood / (Var_neighbourhood + Var_family + pi^2/3); ICC (family) = Var_family / (Var_neighbourhood + Var_family + pi^2/3)

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the variance decomposition conditions on adolescents who lived at home with one or both parents in December 2009, were resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, and had complete register information.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 (flowchart, p. 4); missing data were omitted and not imputed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Estimates from multilevel models are not biased by the small average cluster size (1.3 observations per family and 49.2 per neighbourhood, with many single-observation clusters).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Simulation studies cited by the authors (Bell et al., 2010; Theall et al., 2011).

key_assumptions.assumption: The micro-areas are an adequate operationalisation of the socially meaningful neighbourhood context; a different delineation could yield different general contextual effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors note that the areas used in Urban (2009) and Brattbakk and Wessel (2013) may capture the relevant neighbourhood context better, and that those studies reported higher ICCs.

threats_discussed: The micro-areas may capture the relevant neighbourhood context less well than the areas used in comparable studies, which reported higher ICCs
The neighbourhood context may simply be less important in Denmark than in Sweden or Norway
Earlier studies that did not account for the clustering of families may have overestimated the variance attributed to neighbourhoods
Small average cluster size (1.3 per family, 49.2 per neighbourhood)
Other contexts (school, region) are not included in the nesting structure
robustness_checks: Models stratified by the different age groups showed a slightly lower within family-level variance but no notable heterogeneity across age groups
Sample restricted to individuals at the same address from 2004 to 2009
Outcome redefined as not being in education or employment in two years over 2018-2019

population.description: Persons of Danish origin (native Danes: at least one parent a Danish citizen and born in Denmark) among Danish adolescents aged 10–15 living at home with one or both parents in December 2009
population.selection: Danish adolescent population aged 10–15 in December 2009 living at home with one or both parents, resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, with complete information on all included register variables (Figure 1).

identification.source_of_variation: Observed clustering of individuals within 301,227 families and 7,937 georeferenced micro-area neighbourhoods; the quantity is a variance decomposition of a three-level random-intercept logistic model, not an estimate exploiting exogenous variation.

key_assumptions.assumption: The three-level nesting (individuals in families in neighbourhoods) is correctly specified and the family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts are normally distributed and independent of the model covariates.

The intraclass correlation coefficients are computed with the latent-variable method, fixing the level-1 variance at the variance of the standard logistic distribution (pi squared / 3, approximately 3.29).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Snijders and Bosker (1999), cited in the methods.

formal.as_written: ICC (neighbourhood) = Var_neighbourhood / (Var_neighbourhood + Var_family + pi^2/3); ICC (family) = Var_family / (Var_neighbourhood + Var_family + pi^2/3)

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the variance decomposition conditions on adolescents who lived at home with one or both parents in December 2009, were resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, and had complete register information.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 (flowchart, p. 4); missing data were omitted and not imputed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Estimates from multilevel models are not biased by the small average cluster size (1.3 observations per family and 49.2 per neighbourhood, with many single-observation clusters).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Simulation studies cited by the authors (Bell et al., 2010; Theall et al., 2011).

key_assumptions.assumption: The micro-areas are an adequate operationalisation of the socially meaningful neighbourhood context; a different delineation could yield different general contextual effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors note that the areas used in Urban (2009) and Brattbakk and Wessel (2013) may capture the relevant neighbourhood context better, and that those studies reported higher ICCs.

threats_discussed: The micro-areas may capture the relevant neighbourhood context less well than the areas used in comparable studies, which reported higher ICCs
The neighbourhood context may simply be less important in Denmark than in Sweden or Norway
Earlier studies that did not account for the clustering of families may have overestimated the variance attributed to neighbourhoods
Small average cluster size (1.3 per family, 49.2 per neighbourhood)
Other contexts (school, region) are not included in the nesting structure
robustness_checks: Models stratified by the different age groups showed a slightly lower within family-level variance but no notable heterogeneity across age groups

population.description: Persons of Danish origin (native Danes: at least one parent a Danish citizen and born in Denmark) among Danish adolescents aged 10–15 living at home with one or both parents in December 2009
population.selection: Danish adolescent population aged 10–15 in December 2009 living at home with one or both parents, resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, with complete information on all included register variables (Figure 1).

identification.source_of_variation: Observed clustering of individuals within 301,227 families and 7,937 georeferenced micro-area neighbourhoods; the quantity is a variance decomposition of a three-level random-intercept logistic model, not an estimate exploiting exogenous variation.

key_assumptions.assumption: The three-level nesting (individuals in families in neighbourhoods) is correctly specified and the family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts are normally distributed and independent of the model covariates.

The intraclass correlation coefficients are computed with the latent-variable method, fixing the level-1 variance at the variance of the standard logistic distribution (pi squared / 3, approximately 3.29).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Snijders and Bosker (1999), cited in the methods.

formal.as_written: ICC (neighbourhood) = Var_neighbourhood / (Var_neighbourhood + Var_family + pi^2/3); ICC (family) = Var_family / (Var_neighbourhood + Var_family + pi^2/3)

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the variance decomposition conditions on adolescents who lived at home with one or both parents in December 2009, were resident in Denmark in both 2009 and 2019, and had complete register information.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 1 (flowchart, p. 4); missing data were omitted and not imputed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Estimates from multilevel models are not biased by the small average cluster size (1.3 observations per family and 49.2 per neighbourhood, with many single-observation clusters).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Simulation studies cited by the authors (Bell et al., 2010; Theall et al., 2011).

key_assumptions.assumption: The micro-areas are an adequate operationalisation of the socially meaningful neighbourhood context; a different delineation could yield different general contextual effects.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors note that the areas used in Urban (2009) and Brattbakk and Wessel (2013) may capture the relevant neighbourhood context better, and that those studies reported higher ICCs.

threats_discussed: The micro-areas may capture the relevant neighbourhood context less well than the areas used in comparable studies, which reported higher ICCs
The neighbourhood context may simply be less important in Denmark than in Sweden or Norway
Earlier studies that did not account for the clustering of families may have overestimated the variance attributed to neighbourhoods
Small average cluster size (1.3 per family, 49.2 per neighbourhood)
Other contexts (school, region) are not included in the nesting structure
robustness_checks: Models stratified by the different age groups showed a slightly lower within family-level variance but no notable heterogeneity across age groups
Sample restricted to individuals at the same address from 2004 to 2009
Outcome redefined as not being in education or employment in two years over 2018-2019

estimator.value: Three-level random-intercept logistic regression (Stata 17 'melogit'); random-effect variances with intraclass correlation coefficients, median odds ratios and proportional change in variance

estimation.specification: Model C: adjusted for vulnerable neighbourhoods, gender, age fixed effects, family educational level, family income, family unemployment, family type, children in the family.
fixed_effects: age fixed effects (dummy variables representing the cohorts)
estimation.clustering: No clustered standard errors; non-independence handled by family- and neighbourhood-level random intercepts.
